paragraphs: When a gazelle that has spotted a predator bounds stiffly into the air, all four legs held rigid, it performs a display known as stotting, and the behavior has long puzzled ethologists, since each leap spends energy and time that would seem better devoted to flight. An older explanation held that stotting warns other members of the herd; yet gazelles have been observed stotting when no companions were nearby, a circumstance in which a warning would have no audience. A more persuasive account treats the display as addressed to the predator itself. On this view, a vigorous leap advertises that the animal has detected the hunter and is fit enough to outrun it, and in field studies predators did appear more likely to abandon pursuits of individuals that stotted at high rates. The evidence is not decisive, since healthy animals may simply stot more and also be harder to catch, in which case the display would accompany, rather than cause, the failed pursuit; but the finding is at least what the signaling account predicts.
